articles.title: FSSAI collects samples of major packaged drinking water brands; warns of action in case of violation
articles.summary: New Delhi: Food regulator FSSAI has collected samples of all major packaged drinking water brands, including Bisleri , as part of its ongoing enforcement drive and will take legal action against companies that are non-compliant with its regulations, according to sources. The action against Bisleri International, the leading supplier of packaged drinking water, is part of the ongoing enforcement drive, they added. According to sources, the FSSAI officials have carried out inspections of the premises of food business operators (FBOs) engaged in packaged water business and also took samples for lab testing. The sanction of prosecution against Bisleri International is part of this exercise being undertaken in the public interest, a source said. 'We maintain stringent quality controls': Bisleri responds after FSSAI finds water unsafe FSSAI would take legal action against companies if their sample fail in lab testing and they are found to be violating the rules and regulations, sources said. On Sunday, through a social media post, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) informed that it has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd regarding "unsafe packaged drinking water". A regulatory sample of "Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)" was collected from the premises of Bisleri International for analysis. "The sample was found non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006," the regulator said. Upon appeal by the company, the sample was sent to the referral food laboratory, which also declared it "unsafe" due to the detection of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), the regulator added. The findings of the lab established violations relating to unsafe food under the law. Hence, the FSSAI said it has granted sanction to launch prosecution under the FSS Act, 2006, against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd. On Monday, Bisleri International asserted that its packaged drinking water is "safe" for consumption, and it will cooperate with the food regulator to address the issue. To date, Bisleri said, it has not received any notice by email or in hard copy and has been unable to locate the reported notice on FSSAI's website. "Drinking water safety is a priority for Bisleri. We maintain stringent quality controls of over 90 tests across our 10-step manufacturing process," the company said, while asserting that its product is safe for consumption.

articles.title: Supreme Court rebukes Bihar sessions judge over SP conviction, suggests judicial academy training
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Monday sharply rebuked a Bihar sessions judge for overreaching his authority by convicting a Superintendent of Police (SP) and suggested he undergo training at the National Judicial Academy. A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana rejected the plea by Anil Kumar challenging a Patna High Court order that had termed his actions “unprecedented.” The court told him to stop acting like "Bahubali". The trial judge had summoned and convicted an SP—earlier posted in Rohtak and now in Saran—for failing to comply with a 2023 directive to register a case of false evidence. Supreme Court directs Election Commission to increase strength of West Bengal SIR tribunals, prioritise pleas against deletions In September, he held the officer guilty of criminal contempt and imposed a symbolic fine of Re 1. Justice Bagchi did not mince words, “Your understanding of law is appalling. You took such an aggressive stance, called the Superintendent and convicted him. We appreciate your effort to do justice, but we are governed by procedural constraints and discipline… Enough of adventure. As a judge, you must know your jurisdiction.” The court clarified that non-compliance with a court’s order to register an FIR does not amount to an offence committed in the face of the court and cannot trigger summary criminal contempt proceedings. “We are really surprised at your understanding of law. You must first understand the scope and ambit of Section 384 BNSS and Section 345 CrPC,” the bench observed. “If someone slaps someone or abuses the court, or refuses to leave the courtroom when directed, that is an offence committed in the face of the Court. But if we direct someone to register an FIR and they do not, it does not amount to a crime committed in the face of the court,” the bench said. Supreme Court approves appointment of five retired judges as ad-hoc judges Mocking the overreach, the bench asked if the judge was attempting to act like “Bahubali” and told him to “stay his hands.” The Supreme Court disposed of the petition, allowing the judicial officer to approach the High Court and requesting a sympathetic view.

articles.title: Commission seeks evidence from UP CM Yogi on claim of 1.27 crore missing Hindu voters
articles.summary: An independent commission comprising five retired judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts has written to Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, seeking supporting material and data for his reported claim that 1.27 crore Hindus were excluded from the state's electoral rolls during the Election Commission of India's (ECI) Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise. In a letter dated November 21, the Independent Commission on SIR, proposed by the Lawyers' Association for Constitution (LAFC), said Yogi Adityanath's statement was directly relevant to its mandate of examining whether eligible voters had been unfairly removed from electoral rolls during the revision exercise. The commission has requested the Chief Minister to furnish substantive data, supporting material or information indicating possible gaps in the methodology adopted during the SIR exercise that may have resulted in the alleged deletions. The letter states that the commission would examine the material "with complete autonomy and impartiality" before arriving at its final findings. The communication comes amid a political and administrative debate over the alleged discrepancies between Uttar Pradesh's panchayat electoral rolls and the Election Commission's Assembly electoral rolls, ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections. According to the commission's letter, its mandate extends beyond examining the constitutional and legal validity of the SIR exercise to assessing the methodology adopted and its impact on eligible voters and the final electoral lists, particularly in view of reports of large-scale deletions. The commission has also cited the urgency of the matter, stating that the possible denial of voting rights to millions of electors and the impending elections require the relevant material to be furnished at the earliest. "The Commission is working with a tight timeline and would appreciate if the necessary material is provided at the earliest," the letter stated. Yogi Adityanath had reportedly claimed that 1.27 crore Hindu voters whose names appeared in Uttar Pradesh's panchayat electoral rolls were missing from the Election Commission's electoral rolls following the SIR exercise. The Chief Minister had also referred to 66 lakh voters whose names were allegedly missing, including 55 lakh Hindu beneficiaries of government welfare schemes and approximately 4.5 lakh voters in the 18-19 age group. He had questioned how the names went missing and who was responsible for the alleged discrepancy. However, the Election Commission's position on the religious classification of voters has also become a significant part of the controversy. On November 17, Uttar Pradesh Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa clarified that the Election Commission does not maintain voter data based on religion or caste. He said the electoral database contains details such as voters' names, age, gender, house numbers and family-related information, but does not record their religious or caste identities. Rinwa also pointed out that analyses of voters based on religion conducted by media organisations or independent analysts should not be treated as official Election Commission data. The Independent Commission on SIR is chaired by Justice Madan B Lokur, former judge of the Supreme Court of India. Its other members are Justice AK Patnaik, former Supreme Court judge; Justice Badar Durrez Ahmad, former Chief Justice of the Jammu and Kashmir High Court; Justice Rekha Sharma, former judge of the Delhi High Court; and Justice Anjana Prakash, former judge of the Patna High Court. The commission was constituted as a civil society initiative proposed by the Lawyers' Association for Constitution to examine concerns surrounding the design, implementation and overall impact of the SIR exercise. It has stated that its assessment will draw upon public hearings, empirical and field research, and other verifiable material. The SIR exercise in Uttar Pradesh began on October 27, 2025, and the revised final electoral rolls were published on April 10, 2026. The state's electorate, which stood at approximately 15.44 crore before the exercise, declined to around 13.39 crore following the revision, according to reports. Subsequently, the Election Commission published the draft electoral rolls under the Special Summary Revision (SSR) process on November 17, 2026. According to the Uttar Pradesh Chief Electoral Officer, the draft roll contained 13,58,68,905 electors, including 7,38,58,510 men, 6,20,06,353 women and 4,042 third-gender voters. This represented a net increase of 18,84,113 electors compared with the final electoral roll published after the SIR in April. articles.title: Rohingya in Bangladesh welcome UN court's genocide verdict but say they want to go home to Myanmar
articles.summary: By Shamimul Islam Faisal COX’S BAZAR, Bangladesh (AP) — Hundreds of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh sat in front of a big screen at their sprawling camp in Cox’s Bazar, watching the news from the Netherlands, where the U.N.'s top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation. For many, the historic verdict on Thursday represented a “small victory” — offering a glimmer of hope that someday they would be able to return safely to their homes in Myanmar, across the border from Bangladesh . Only then, some said, will they be “fully satisfied.” It was a landmark judgment, finding Myanmar responsible for the crime against the country’s ethnic Rohingya — the first time the court ruled that a state committed genocide. The Hague-based International Court of Justice also ordered Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow the Rohingya to return home safely, pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide. But it remains to be seen how much of the ruling can be implemented. The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council. Myanmar’s government on Friday dismissed the ruling as “unfair.” Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman, who is also president of the U.N. General Assembly, went to Cox’s Bazar on Friday to tell Rohingyas who fled the genocide in Myanmar that “at this historic moment” there must be action, his U.N. spokesperson said. Suspects must be prosecuted, Rohingya must be able to return to Myanmar voluntarily and safely, they must receive reparations and Myanmar’s government must ensure there will never be another genocide, Rahman said, according to spokesperson Melissa Summers. He also said he will advocate with U.N. member nations on how to follow up on the judgment, stressing “You will not be alone,” she said. At the refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar on Thursday, Rohingya refugees told The Associated Press of their concerns. Mohammad Rofik, a Rohingya community leader at the camp, said the verdict was “a victory” for them as it recognized the genocide and the suffering of their minority in the Buddhist-majority nation, but that it was “not an end” to their ordeal. “Justice has started,” Rofik said, adding that the Rohingya still have “a long way to go.” For Sayed Ullah, another Rohingya community leader, the verdict was a historic recognition that the Rohingya are a distinct ethnic group. “Myanmar denies the existence of the Rohingya, but now the (U.N.) court made it clear," he said. Other refugees reacted sharply, saying that the international community should punish Myanmar authorities. “The court has stated and established that genocide was committed against the Rohingya people," said Mohammad Osman, a Rohingya refugee. "Based on this ruling, the entire Rohingya community is calling on ... (the world) to impose severe punishment on Myanmar.” In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes. The Hague-based court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya. Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part.” About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions. Bangladesh has been urging the international community to help repatriate the refugees.

articles.title: Rights groups urge sanctions after top UN court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
articles.summary: By Edith M. Lederer Rights groups are calling for military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court, in the first ruling of its kind, determined that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation. The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling , which orders Myanmar’s military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide. Myanmar’s government has denied committing genocide, claiming it acted against insurgents, and is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court’s demands. President Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the 2017 operation. The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 100,000 Rohingya. Khine Khine Soe, the president's spokeswoman, noted the International Court of Justice decision handed down Thursday had been the result of a nine-to-six vote of the judges. “Not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she told reporters in the capital Naypyitaw. “So it was not a decision made unanimously. I would say that it was unfair.” While the World Court’s rulings are final and legally binding, it has no recourse beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council. UN Security Council has the power to impose sanctions The Security Council scheduled closed consultations on the ruling next Wednesday and a private meeting on Dec. 7 at the request of the United Kingdom, which expelled Myanmar's defense attache after Thursday's ruling. But Daniel Forti, the International Crisis Group’s head of U.N. affairs, said it’s unlikely there will be any immediate action from the 15-member Security Council, which could impose sanctions on Myanmar. He said any action would likely be blocked by China and Russia, both permanent members with veto power. “China has discouraged the Security Council from acting on the Myanmar file since 2021, as it is reluctant to cede any influence in its own backyard,” Forti told The Associated Press. “The ICJ ruling will not alter China’s calculations, and it is hard to imagine that either Beijing or Moscow would support any potential Security Council resolution that attempts to enforce the court’s recommendations.” Forti said Gambia, which launched the court proceedings, may eventually pursue a resolution in the 193-member General Assembly calling on Myanmar to comply with the ICJ’s demands, even though its actions are not legally binding, unlike those of the Security Council. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman plans to hold “an informal dialogue” with the U.N.’s 193 member nations on the ICJ ruling and remains open to other exchanges, assembly spokesperson Melissa Summers said. Rahman, who is also Bangladesh’s foreign minister, went to Cox’s Bazaar Friday and told a crowd of Rohingya “at this historic moment” that there must be action and pledged to be their voice in New York, she said. Justice for All, an American human rights organization that advocates for the rights of Muslim minorities, called on the Trump administration to support a General Assembly resolution demanding Myanmar’s compliance with the judgment, and establishing international monitoring and follow-up. Rights groups call for targeting Myanmar's economy and military Justice for All, which has a task force of 38 U.S. and Canadian Muslim organizations that have advocated for Rohingya rights since 2017, argued that sanctions should target Myanmar’s oil and gas sector and the networks that provide weapons and other support to its military. Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnes Callamard urged governments not to welcome the president “on the international stage, especially as grave violations continue unchecked inside Myanmar.” “Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar,” she said. “The U.N. Security Council should impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court.” That court, however, is under U.S. sanctions along with many of its judges and staff, so any action by the Security Council would face an almost certain U.S. veto. Prosecutors at the ICC requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing in late 2024 alleging he was responsible for crimes against humanity against the Rohingya. There has been no public announcement on a decision by judges at the court who would have to issue a warrant. The court's Office of the Prosecutor said in an email response to questions from The Associated Press that the ICJ judgment “will not have any bearing on matters that are currently before the Judges of the ICC,” and noted that the ICC deals with allegations of individual criminal responsibility of people, as opposed to state responsibility. No clear path for reparations for the Rohingya Human Rights Watch urged governments to step forward to help the Rohingya. “Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” Maria Elena Vignoli, the group's senior international justice counsel, said in a statement. Justice for All called for global support for a Rohingya reparations fund and measures to advance their education, protection, pursuit of citizenship and safe voluntary return from Bangladesh, where some 1.2 million Rohingya now live in overcrowded camps. Myanmar, which is majority Buddhist, has long claimed the Rohingya are “Bengali” migrants from Bangladesh, even though their families have lived in the country for generations. Nearly all Rohingya have been denied citizenship since 1982, effectively rendering them stateless, and they are denied freedom of movement and other basic rights. Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who listened to the court ruling in The Hague, Netherlands, said the judgment “will only mean something if governments act on it.” “So, I say to every U.N. member state, take robust steps to implement the ICJ judgment,” she said, starting with sanctions against the president. “Make Myanmar pay reparations to the people it destroyed,” she said. “Give us back our lives. Give us a future. We want to be part of a stable, prosperous and thriving Myanmar.”

articles.title: The history of the persecution of Myanmar’s Rohingya
articles.summary: Some 420,000 Rohingya Muslims, a religious and ethnic minority community in Myanmar, have fled to neighboring Bangladesh since August this year. The United Nations has called the Rohingya the world’s most persecuted minority group and described the atrocities by Myanmar’s authorities as “ ethnic cleansing ,” whereby one group removes another ethnic or religious community through violence. But the persecution of the Rohingya is not new. My research on the Rohingya Muslim experience in Myanmar shows that this pattern of persecution goes back to 1948 – the year when the country achieved independence from their British colonizers. Here is their brief history. The legacy of colonialism The British ruled Myanmar (then Burma) for over a century, beginning with a series of wars in 1824 . Colonial policies encouraged migrant labor in order to increase rice cultivation and profits. Many Rohingya entered Myanmar as part of these policies in the 17th century. According to census records , between 1871 to 1911, the Muslim population tripled. The British also promised the Rohingya separate land – a “ Muslim National Area ” – in exchange for support. During the Second World War , for example, the Rohingya sided with the British while Myanmar’s nationalists supported the Japanese. Following the war, the British rewarded the Rohingya with prestigious government posts. However, they were not given an autonomous state. In 1948, when Myanmar achieved independence from the British, violent conflicts broke out among various segments of its more than one hundred ethnic and racial groups. Decades-long persecution After independence, the Rohingya asked for the promised autonomous state, but officials rejected their request. Calling them foreigners, they also denied them citizenship. These animosities continued to grow. Many in Myanmar saw the Rohingya as having benefited from colonial rule. A nationalist movement and Buddhist religious revival further contributed to the growing hatred. In 1950, some Rohingya staged a rebellion against the policies of the Myanmar government. They demanded citizenship; they also asked for the state that had been promised them. Ultimately the army crushed the resistance movement. Where Rohingyas live The majority of Rohingyas live in the Rakhine state in Myanmar. Much like today’s terrorists, the rebels at the time were called “ Mujahid ” or engaged in “struggle” or “jihad.” It is important to point out that the international community has never agreed on how to define “terrorism.” The legal definition could vary by country as politics dictates its contours. As scholar Ben Saul says , officials can use its meaning as a weapon against even valid political rivals. The lack of consensus, as Saul argues, reflects disagreement about what violence is legitimate, when and by whom. In 1962, just over a decade later, a military coup culminated in a one-party military state where democratic governance was woefully lacking. During the next 60 years of military rule, things worsened for the Rohingya. The authorities saw the minority group as a threat to nationalist identity . Calling them foreigners, the army killed, tortured and raped. They closed Rohingya social and political organizations. They also transfered private Rohingya businesses to the government, debilitating the group financially. Further, the Rohingya suffered forced labor, arbitrary detention and physical assaults. In 1991 and 1992, more than 250,000 attempted to escape to Bangladesh. Rohingya ‘statelessness’ In 1977, when the army launched a national drive to register citizens, the Rohingya were considered illegal. More than 200,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh at the time because of further atrocities. Authorities pointed to their flight as purported evidence of their illegal status. The Citizenship Act of Myanmar, enacted in 1982, formally denied the group citizenship rights. This law required that a person’s ancestors belong to a national race or group present in Myanmar prior to British rule in 1823, to become a citizen. The Rohingya were still classified as illegal immigrants allowed in by British colonizers. As Human Rights Watch has noted, however, their presence actually dates back to the 12th century . Today, the Rohingya are the single largest “ stateless ” community in the world. Their “statelessness” or lack of citizenship increases their vulnerability because they are not entitled to any legal protection from the government. Without citizenship, they are deprived of basic rights such as access to health services, education and employment. The illiteracy rate among the Rohingya, for example, is a staggering 80 percent. Additionally, they have been denied the right to worship freely. They also face restrictions on the right to marry, move freely and own property because of their religious and ethnic identity. Even though Rohingya population growth has slowed down , anxieties not only persist but are codified in law : Rohingya couples are allowed no more than two children. Those who break the law risk imprisonment, and the government blacklists their children. Without legal status, they cannot go to school, travel or buy property. The police can also arrest and imprison them. The current crisis Despite Myanmar’s recent democratic transition, the persecution persists. The current humanitarian catastrophe ostensibly began with an assault on police posts by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army , a new insurgency group . Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh told Human Rights Watch that Myanmar government forces had carried out armed attacks, and burned down their homes. In addition, they beheaded men , raped women and murdered children . Tens of thousands of Rohingya have become internally displaced. Even prior to this crisis, 120,000 displaced Rohingya had been living in internment camps. A burnt house in Rakhine state of Myanmar, where majority of Rohingya live. Amnesty International said there were indications that authorities in Myanmar have also placed illegal landmines at locations commonly used by refugees Among those killed were two children. What is more, international humanitarian aid has been blocked , preventing necessities like food, water and medicine from reaching a quarter of a million people. Aung San Suu Kyi and human rights The Myanmar Army, meanwhile, denies any wrongdoing. Despite the global outcry, they claim to be conducting “ counterterrorism ” operations. Due to the severity of the human rights crisis, however, the British government decided to stop its defense engagement and training of the military in Myanmar. None of this criticism, however, has made Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar’s de facto leader and Nobel laureate, acknowledge the plight of the Rohingya. Amid international criticism, she recently canceled her visit to this week’s U.N. General Assembly in New York. In her speech to Myanmar’s parliament, she denied that there had been any “armed clashes or clearance operations” since September 5, this year. Tragically, her actions signal there will be no end to the persecution of Rohingya anytime soon. Myanmar’s leader Aung San Suu Kyi addresses the nation on the Rohingya situation.

articles.title: Premium theft? Delhi duo buy gold tickets to Diljit Dosanjh's Ahmedabad concert to 'target rich people'
articles.summary: In an unexpected turn of events, two men from Delhi allegedly bought high-end Gold class tickets for Diljit Dosanjh's Ahmedabad concert to target rich people and steal their expensive phones. The two men, who were identified by the police as Mohammad Gulzar and Ashraf Hussain Idrishi, travelled to Ahmedabad to attend Dosanjh's concert at the Narendra Modi Stadium, with the sole intention of stealing expensive smartphones. As per a report by The Economic Times , the Ahmedabad Local Crime Branch has arrested the accused and recovered 11 mobile phones worth Rs 4.3 lakh approximately. Police suspect the accused may be linked to around six theft cases. Delhi Police denies permission to Diljit Dosanjh's October 30 concert over security concerns The two accused reportedly bought gold-category tickets to orchestrate the high-profile theft, believing that only rich people with high-end and expensive phones will buy those tickets. As per reports, several concertgoers flagged their missing mobile phones to the stadium's control room, prompting officials to launch an investigation and deploy a security team at the venue's exit gates to identify suspicious individuals. Once the concert ended, the two accused reportedly tried to flee the spot after spotting the security team and was later detained by the police. Further investigation into the matter is currently underway. 'Why the double standards?': Diljit Dosanjh cites Coldplay to slam lyrics curb at Ahmedabad concert Dosanjh performed at the Narendra Modi Stadium on November 21, 2026, as part of his AURA India Tour. During the concert, the Lover singer took a swipe at the critics who had objected to some of his songs claiming that they promote alcohol and substance use. Ahead of his performance, Dosanjh while calling out the double standards, questioned why it is acceptable for artists like Coldplay to sing lyrics involving alcohol, yet becomes problematic when he does the same. The four songs that sparked objections were Patiala Peg, Panj Tara, Je Bichcho Feem Labbiya and Jatt Utthe Fire Karda .

articles.summary: New Delhi: Former India pacer Irfan Pathan is confident that Mahendra Singh Dhoni will not be sitting at the auction table when Chennai Super Kings (CSK) pick their squad for IPL 2027, saying the veteran's role will be to mentor players rather than get involved in the bidding process. The IPL auction will be held in Goa on December 16. Dhoni's IPL playing career came to an end earlier this month, with his appointment as CSK's mentor after he expressed his desire to retire during a video call to discuss player retentions for the upcoming season. 'There is no CSK without MS Dhoni': Iconic player retires from IPL, named team mentor Mahendra Singh Dhoni relives glorious career through nostalgic montage 'Thala' Dhoni retires from IPL | Quick glance at milestones of CSK legend Dhoni played for CSK in 17 of the 19 IPL seasons between 2008 and 2026. He was part of the franchise in every season except 2016 and 2017, when CSK were suspended and he turned out for Rising Pune Supergiant. "Knowing Dhoni, I don't think he will be sitting at the auction table. He is the mentor, sitting at the auction table is not his role. His job is to guide the players, pass on his experience to them, help them perform and teach them how to win matches for CSK. The bidding and the auction decisions are left to the management," said Pathan on JioStar. "He likes to keep things simple and let the people who know the job do it. CSK have a strong management and a think tank that have built title-winning squads for years, and Dhoni has always trusted them completely," said Pathan, referring to the five-time IPL-winning captain. Pathan said Dhoni had never been one to seek the limelight or take credit for off-field decisions and would prefer to work quietly behind the scenes in his new role. "So, I would be surprised if we see him sitting at CSK's auction table. He will be involved in his own way as a mentor, but it will be behind the scenes, not at the auction table," opined Pathan. CSK have missed the playoffs in each of the last three seasons, and former India batter Abhinav Mukund felt the franchise's gamble on youth had failed to pay off, with several expensive buys not delivering. "The gamble on youth hasn't paid off for CSK. Prashant Veer was bought for Rs 14.2 crore and didn't deliver, though you can't blame him much since he barely got to bowl. He's been released, so the money has come in," said Mukund. "Kartik Sharma, the other 14-crore buy, played some match-winning knocks and has been retained. But CSK still have a surplus of Indian top-order batters. They can't fit Ruturaj Gaikwad, Sanju Samson, Ayush Mhatre, Dewald Brevis, Kartik Sharma, Urvil Patel and Sarfaraz Khan into one playing XI." Mukund identified bowling as CSK's biggest concern and felt the franchise could use its surplus of batters to strengthen that department at the auction. "Their main issue is the bowling. With Liam Livingstone's arrival, him, (Dewald) Brevis, and Noor Ahmad are sure starters, and the last overseas spot is likely Jamie Overton's. That makes it hard for Akeal Hosein and Noor to play together. "CSK are looking for an Indian spinner, their bowling looks thin, but they have batters to offer. If a team wants to trade a bowler, CSK can give a batter in return and I can firmly see them bolstering their bowling at the auction," he added.

Myanmar genocide ruling is a watershed moment in international justice – with huge ramifications for other cases
articles.summary: The International Court of Justice’s historic ruling of genocide against Myanmar on Nov. 19, 2026, will have significant consequences for the parties involved in the case – and potentially some who are not. The Hague’s highly anticipated judgment in Gambia v. Myanmar is a major victory for Gambia, the tiny west African nation that filed a complaint with the court against Myanmar in 2019. It is also a major moment of accountability for the military leadership of Myanmar. But as an expert in genocide and mass atrocity prevention, I believe the ruling goes far beyond these nations. Indeed, it is also a watershed moment for international legal justice that is bound to have important effects on the court’s other ongoing genocide cases, particularly the case of South Africa v. Israel . Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on Nov. What the court ruled Gambia’s case focused on actions that Myanmar’s military government called “clearance operations” in the course of its decades-long violent persecution of the country’s Muslim Rohingya minority . The Tatmadaw , as the Myanmar military is known, justified these actions as a counterinsurgency operation. Yet in the course of those attacks, soldiers were found to have destroyed hundreds of Rohingya villages , and to have committed widespread rapes, torture and summary killings. While the precise death toll of the 2017 attacks may never be known, at least 10,000 Rohingya civilians are thought to have died , and roughly 750,000 Rohingya fled to neighboring Bangladesh. There they joined other Rohingya in what is now the world’s largest refugee camp of over 1.2 million people, comprised of those who had already fled years of the Myanmar government’s persecution and attacks. The court’s ruling that the Tatmadaw’s attacks amounted to genocide rested on its interpretation of the crime of genocide in the 1948 U.N. Genocide Convention , the first major international treaty approved by the United Nations General Assembly. For an attack to be genocidal, it must be directed against an ethnic, religious, racial or national group, and must include at least one of five prohibited acts: killing members of a group; inflicting serious physical or mental harm on members; deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about its destruction; imposing measures intended to prevent births; or forcibly transferring children from the group. Beyond these factual requirements, genocide requires that the perpetrator specifically intended these acts to destroy the group, in whole or in part. Rohingya: A persecuted people Rakhine State in western Myanmar is home to the majority of the nation's Rohingya minority. Hundreds of thousands cross the border to Bangladesh during the genocide. Map: The Conversation, CC-BY-NDCreated with Datawrapper In its ruling, the court agreed that the facts of Myanmar’s attacks met the legal definition of genocide. For the notoriously difficult and demanding requirement for proving the “ special intent ” to destroy a group, the court determined that the pattern, selective targeting and lethality of the attacks on Rohingya villages could not plausibly be explained as a counterinsurgency operation. Instead, the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the military’s actions, the court determined, was the specific intent to destroy the Rohingya ethnic minority. A series of historic firsts The court’s decision is unprecedented in many important respects. In an influential previous ruling on violations of the Genocide Convention, in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro in 2007, the court found only that Serbia had not met its legal duty to prevent genocide by failing to use its influence to restrain the Bosnian Serb army in the Srebrenica massacre of 1995 . In the Myanmar ruling, by contrast, the court ruled for the first time that a country is legally responsible for committing genocide – not merely failing to prevent it. Further, the court ruled for the first time that a country that has committed genocide also has multiple obligations toward the victim group. Those include designing and implementing a comprehensive program of reparations and compensation for victims; creating conditions where Rohingya can make a safe, voluntary and dignified return to their homes; and restoration of their citizenship status after national legislation from 1982 rendered them stateless . Rohingya Refugees cross a river at Tambru, a no-man’s land on the Bangladesh-Myanmar border. Finally, the court also demanded that Myanmar take steps to investigate all those involved in the genocide to determine individual criminal responsibility. Since the International Court of Justice is not a criminal court and only hears cases between states, this order explicitly connects the ruling to other courts where individual perpetrators can be held accountable. These include the International Criminal Court – which had already requested an arrest warrant for Tatmadaw leader Min Aung Hlaing – as well as national courts that may pursue prosecution according to the doctrine of universal jurisdiction. The ruling’s broader implications The court’s ruling in Gambia vs. Myanmar is also likely to have huge ramifications far beyond the case itself. In filing its complaint, Gambia appealed to an innovative argument to establish that it had legal standing. It argued for what’s known as “ erga omnes partes ,” roughly translated as “toward all parties to a treaty.” According to this line of reasoning, the Genocide Convention imposes such strong legal duties to prevent and punish the crime of genocide that any state, even one that has not in any way been directly harmed, has the standing – in fact, the obligation – to seek legal remedies. In accepting Gambia’s “erga omnes partes” approach, the court opened a pathway for other cases centering on violations of the Genocide Convention. Of these, the most significant by far is the ongoing case of South Africa v. Israel , which charges the Israeli government and the Israeli military of committing genocide against Palestinian civilians in the Gaza Strip. Going forward, other nations would now also have a legal tool for holding perpetrator states accountable for committing the most serious international crimes. The International Court of Justice has no enforcement arm. As such, the Myanmar government cannot be compelled to abide by its rulings, whether to cease any further attacks or persecution on the Rohingya, make efforts to repatriate them or design a comprehensive reparation and compensation plan. But even if Myanmar chooses to ignore the court’s specific orders, the ruling is a major defeat. The reputational damage of being the first country found guilty of state-sponsored genocide is likely to be considerable. Further, the ruling will support claims that other nations have a duty not to assist Myanmar in any way that might support or enable further attacks on Rohingya. While that doesn’t automatically mean other countries will fulfill their duties under international law, many are nonetheless likely to use the ruling to bolster multilateral efforts to impose political, economic and social costs on the Tatmadaw. That could include targeted economic sanctions, financial restrictions, prohibitions on arms sales and other forms of cooperation with Myanmar’s government. The ruling thus comes with a potentially hefty price tag for the military junta. Given the general weakening of international legal institutions over the past 20 years, a dysfunctional U.N. Security Council and an International Criminal Court under siege by the Trump administration , the court’s ruling is a rare victory for international justice and opens new routes for international genocide prevention and accountability efforts. Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice at a camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on Nov. 19, 2026. Before all else, though, it is also a victory for the Rohingya – a people who have suffered decades of persecution. Thousands gathered in their Bangladeshi refugee camps to watch and cheer as the court’s president, Judge Iwasawa Yuji, read the court’s judgment. Camp inhabitants held aloft signs and chanted a simple message as the verdict came down: “Thank you Gambia.”

articles.title: We want only BS6 vehicles in Delhi, says Supreme Court amid air pollution crisis
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Monday said it was considering allowing only BS-VI vehicles in the national capital, as it expressed concern over the recurring air pollution crisis in Delhi-NCR during a hearing on air pollution . A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was hearing a suo motu case examining the regulatory framework governing air pollution. "We are clear; we want only BS6 vehicles in Delhi, if not NCR," Justice Bagchi remarked during the hearing. Supreme Court terms vehicular emissions major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR Pollution in Delhi-NCR: Sharp increase in vehicular emissions warrants urgent intervention, says Supreme Court BS6 (Bharat Stage 6) vehicles are motor vehicles manufactured, sold and registered in India that comply with strict emission standards introduced on April 1, 2020. They align closely with Euro 6 norms and significantly cut harmful exhaust pollutants compared to older BS4 vehicles. The top court also stressed the need for a long-term plan to prevent polluting commercial vehicles from entering Delhi while ensuring uninterrupted supplies of essential commodities. "Why not (and) how to ensure that commercial vehicles don't enter Delhi at all? But it does not mean that Delhi people don't require (those). They have a lot of necessities. They require vegetables, fruits, other day-to-day items. So, everything will have to be available. So what can be the alternative? "Can there be something that… at the border, some warehouse so that you have some other battery-operated vehicles or non-polluting vehicles to bring them inside the city? This kind of arrangement may not be possible this year, may not be possible next year. But why not have this during five years? To ensure that no single commercial vehicle enters Delhi," the CJI remarked. During the brief hearing, the apex court also sought accountability from NCR states over the issue of air pollution and questioned why they were not actively participating in this process. It directed Haryana, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and other states concerned to file status reports detailing steps taken to reduce particulate pollution across the NCR. Expressing serious concern over the recurring air pollution crisis in Delhi-NCR, the top court had earlier termed vehicular emissions a major contributor to the deteriorating air quality and asked authorities why the air quality index continues to remain alarming despite several regulatory measures. The bench had highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad.

articles.title: Rupee tumbles 30 paise to settle at 92.92 against US dollar
articles.summary: Mumbai: The rupee lost 30 paise to settle at 92.92 (provisional) against the US dollar on Monday, reversing its five-day rally, dragged down by a massive sell-off in domestic stock markets. Lower crude oil prices and a softening American currency failed to support the local currency, which faced intense volatility amid a global stock market rout, forex traders said. At the interbank foreign exchange market, the rupee opened at 92.47 and climbed up to 92.43 initially. But it lost ground and hit the day's low at 93.11 before ending the session at 92.92 (provisional) against the greenback, down 30 paise from its previous close. On Friday, the rupee appreciated for the fifth consecutive session to settle 70 paise higher at 92.62 against the US dollar. The Indian unit reclaimed above the 93 level for the first time since April 10. Rupee slide pushes Namma Metro's finance costs above revenue The local unit has logged a sharp appreciation of over 1.6 per cent in the past five back-to-back sessions since the closing level of 94.19 against the greenback recorded on November 13. Anuj Choudhary, Research Analyst, Mirae Asset Sharekhan, said the rupee reversed morning gains on a sharp fall in domestic equity markets. However, softening of the US dollar and a decline in the US Treasury yields cushioned the downside, while crude oil prices too were weak. "Easing of the dollar index from a 19-month high on trimming odds of a 50 bps rate hike by the Fed in December may also support the rupee. However, any further correction in domestic markets may cap a sharp upside. Traders may take cues from PMI data from the US. USD-INR spot price is expected to trade in a range of Rs 92.70 to Rs 93.30," Choudhary said. Meanwhile, the dollar index, which gauges the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was at 103.69, lower by 0.05 per cent. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, was trading 0.53 per cent lower at USD 92.08 per barrel in futures trade. articles.title: Check your labels: Keralam teens' kidney damage put spotlight on mercury in skin creams
articles.summary: A 17-year-old girl from Kerala developed multiple health complications, including kidney damage , after using a skin cream allegedly containing excessive mercury levels in the formulation. The Areakode police registered the girl’s complaint on Sunday night. The FIR stated that the girl purchased and used a cream marketed as "F Tune" after coming across its advertisement on Instagram, PTI reported. The product, easily available in India, claims to remove pimples, facial blemishes, and give skin a glowing appearance. According to the FIR, the cream contained excessive amounts of mercury, a substance extremely harmful to human health.​ She reportedly purchased the cream after seeing a vlogger promoting the product online. The cream is promoted by several influencers online suggesting that the cream is suitable for all skin types and amazing results within a short period of time. A few months back, a dermatologist @drmadhu raised concerned about the products. He pointed out that the product claimed to treat all skin problems and called it a red flag. Moreover, the product label listed ingredients but did not state their concentration levels. Besides the Kerala-based girl, singer Saleem Kodathoor also claimed he suffered from kidney disease after using a skin-lightening cream. He said it happened nearly 10 years ago and required treatment for several months in a video on social media.​ View this post on Instagram Why does mercury appear in cosmetics?​ Researchers explain that mercury blocks the skin from producing melanin, a natural pigment that gives skin its natural colour. Due to this, the dark spots start to fade, making the skin look noticeably lighter.​ Customers often want fast results, but safe ingredients take time to show results. Certain companies take advantage of this consumer behaviour by sneaking high amounts of mercury into their products so that people see dramatic results within a short time. It gives them an edge over their competitors. Moreover, mercury is very cheap and easy to procure; the health damage it causes also builds silently over many years. People do not end up realising that they are slowly poisoning themselves.​ What do the rules say?​ Cosmetics imported or manufactured in India can contain mercury in the following proportions under the Cosmetics Rules 2020, by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO). In cosmetics intended for use in the eye area, the level of mercury cannot exceed 0.007 per cent. Meanwhile, in other cosmetic products, unintentional mercury levels cannot exceed one part per million (1 ppm). The use of lead and arsenic compounds for the purpose of colouring cosmetics is prohibited.​ The laboratory test results of F Tune reportedly revealed that the mercury level was 1.25 per cent, nearly 12,000 times higher than the permissible level. Case against skin cream producer after girl suffers kidney damage in Keralam Why is mercury dangerous for health?​ Mercury in skincare products is most commonly found in those claiming to help with skin-lightening, brightening, and anti-ageing creams. The toxic metal can cause serious kidney damage, harm to the nervous system, and skin issues through absorption or vapour inhalation.​ A 2025 research article explains that mercury can accumulate in the kidneys and damage their filtering units. This can cause protein in the urine (proteinuria), fluid retention and swelling (especially in the legs, ankles, and feet), blood pressure changes, and conditions such as membranous nephropathy or minimal change disease.​ The metal is a potential neurotoxin which can also cause tremors, irritability, mood changes, depression, memory problems, difficulty concentrating, coordination issues, numbness, and peripheral neuropathy.​ Pregnant women who have prolonged exposure to these products can also put their unborn baby or infants at risk of developmental harm.​ What should a consumer look out for? The United States Food and Drug Administration (US FDA) urges people to check labels, especially on skin lightening and anti-ageing products. "Check the label. If the words "mercurous chloride," "calomel," "mercuric," "mercurio," or "mercury" are listed on the label, mercury is in it—and you should stop using the product immediately." ( With inputs from PTI)

articles.title: Cop31: Why the UN climate summit ended in victory for fossil fuel producing nations
articles.summary: The UN’s annual two-week climate summit, Cop31 , has ended in failure. Countries could not find consensus on a final agreement. It is the first such failure in more than 20 years. The summit started relatively smoothly. In fact, the conference agenda was adopted within a few hours on day one, as country parties found nothing objectionable. At the time, this event looked like it might be smooth sailing: another summit simply focused on implementing policies agreed in previous years. But week two became explosive. First, the draft agreement – which if adopted would have been known as the Antalya Accords – conceded that we have failed to keep global temperature rise below 1.5˚C and that the world is entering a period of “overshoot” . Second, oil and gas producing nations fought to keep the root cause of climate change – namely fossil fuels – out of any deal. And they succeeded, as the agreement fell through. The frustration felt by many was summed up on day ten (November 19) by Panamanian environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro, who said: “While we listen to endless oratory, the planet is being destroyed.” The country’s delegation then said enough is enough – they were not about to put their name to an outcome that does not adequately address the crisis. We are climate experts at UCL who have written about the outcome of these summits for The Conversation since Cop26 in Glasgow , and we were in Antalya this year too. Here’s why we think this year’s summit failed. Disagreement over ‘fossil fuels’ caused the collapse Every Cop meeting since 2003 has resulted in a global agreement. This year, however, countries failed to reach consensus on a final deal, after negotiations broke down over whether to explicitly address fossil fuels. Inside the negotiation rooms at Cop31 in Turkey. The draft agreement presented to the summit for approval omitted any mention of fossil fuels, after pressure from oil, gas and coal producing nations led by Saudi Arabia. The EU, Panama and many vulnerable island nations refused to agree to any text that did not explicitly address them. This disagreement ultimately prevented the summit from reaching consensus. This has been the modus operandi of these summits – they start with a more ambitious draft text that gets weakened as it comes closer to adoption. Last year at Cop30 in Brazil countries agreed a watered-down text with no mention of fossil fuels just to get an agreement. But removing fossil fuels from a climate text is like removing mention of cigarettes in an anti-smoking campaign – it was simply too much for many countries to accept. A push for electrification, without a fossil fuel phase-out There were some positives to come out of the summit. Electrification was a key focus this year, for instance. In this context, it refers to using electricity in transport, industry and other sectors, rather than burning fossil fuels. The summit hosts said the target was 35x35 electrification: making electricity account for 35% of the world’s final energy consumption by 2035. In the last days of the summit, an electrification delivery package was launched with support from more than 150 countries plus the EU, as well as 37 cities and 150 businesses. This included plans for power utilities and energy companies to investment US$156 billion (£119 billion) a year in renewables and energy storage. But electrifying transport and industry will only cut emissions if the electricity itself is clean. Countries pushing for a shift to renewable-powered electrification also wanted a clearer commitment to moving away from fossil fuels. With the negotiations ending without agreement, there was no collective commitment to ensuring electrification would reduce dependence on fossil fuels. The most climate-vulnerable nations were left disappointed Pacific island nations were left deeply disappointed. Many are low-lying coral atolls, where sea-level rise and increasingly severe storms, floods and other extreme weather are threatening their very existence. Cclimate minister of Tuvalu (highest point: 4.6 metres above sea level), Maina Vakafua Talia, is stone faced as Cop31 fails to reach agreement. But Cop31’s failure to agree on stronger action on fossil fuels or adequate adaptation finance exposed the widening gap between what vulnerable countries need and what international negotiations are delivering. Countries have very different responsibilities for tackling climate change. Small island states and least developed countries like the Marshall Islands have emitted very little in the past and have very little to mitigate today. The largest emitters and fossil fuel producers, meanwhile, have a much greater responsibility. Ambassador Albon Ishoda of the Marshall Islands said : “Disappointing is probably not strong enough a word … We have money for wars but not to save communities.” In short, this was an “implementation Cop” which turned into one of the worst ever climate summits. As the world enters a period of overshooting 1.5˚C, the failure to agree on a clear path away from fossil fuels is a big win for the countries that produce them – and another setback for those least responsible for climate change but most exposed to it.

articles.title: Going to the park once a week or more has a measurable impact on a child’s mental health – new study
articles.summary: Child mental health issues have been rising in the UK over the last decade . This was exacerbated by the COVID pandemic and continues to be a concern, particularly around issues such as sedentary lifestyles and excessive screen time. In a new study , colleagues and I have found that visiting a local park regularly had a measurable impact on child mental health . Throughout childhood and through adolescence, children are developing their social and emotional skills. This social-emotional development provides the foundation for good mental health. Failing to reach typical milestones such as developing social skills and friendships provides an indication of a child’s current mental health, as well as their mental health in later life. This means that finding ways to facilitate and encourage healthy social-emotional development is a way to improve child mental health and give them the foundation for good mental health throughout their lives. Having green and natural spaces close to people’s homes is one factor which previous studies have shown is linked with improved child mental health. These spaces are thought to improve child mental health by encouraging healthy behaviour. For example, they encourage physical activity, socialising and imaginative and adventurous play. Research suggests that being in natural spaces can have restorative and stress-reducing effects for both children and adults . Much of the research related to green spaces and child mental health has been cross-sectional study designs. This means that the study measurements are taken at a single point in time, rather than following children over time. While these studies are good at discovering factors which are linked to each other, such as natural spaces and child mental health, they cannot determine whether it was the natural space, or other factors that impacted child mental health. These studies also typically measure residential proximity to green and natural spaces, rather than measuring how often children are actually taken to these spaces. What we did in our study For our study , we chose to focus on visiting parks, as we thought this was likely to enable many of the ways that research has suggested green and natural spaces could improve mental health. We used data from the Children of the 90s study , also known as Alspac (Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children), where information was collected about 14,062 children born in and around the English city of Bristol from the early 1990s to the present day. We used data on children’s visits to parks, as well as their mental health, behaviours and family circumstances from birth to 11 years old. Spending time in parks is beneficial for children. We found that children who were taken to the park at least once a week from six months to 11 years old scored, on average, 16.5% better on their mental health assessments compared to those who were taken less than once a week over the same period. As we had repeated measurements of visiting parks and mental health, we were also able to understand the impact of going to parks on specific children, rather than only comparing groups of children who visited more and less. We found children tended to display better mental health during periods when they went to parks more often compared to when they went less. This provides stronger evidence than a cross-sectional study because it displays change within an individual. These findings remained after accounting for disadvantageous family circumstances such as poor housing and maternal mental health, which are known to affect child mental health. The findings were also unchanged when we carried out sensitivity analyses. This is where we change elements of the study, such as what measures we include in the statistical model or which study participants we include in the sample, to see if it affects the results. When the results are consistent across sensitivity analyses, this gives more confidence in them. We also investigated differences in the frequency of park visits for different groups. Children from more advantaged families were taken to parks more often when they were younger, but as children got older this pattern changed. Some children from less advantaged families were taken to parks more often. Many children were taken to the park less than once a week for all or parts of their childhood. Our results suggest increasing opportunities to visit parks in childhood could improve children’s mental health and reduce inequalities. But reducing inequalities in children’s mental health is only likely to be possible if good quality parks are available, safe, welcoming and easy for all families to use.

articles.title: How your body clock affects your mental health and ways to keep it in sync
articles.summary: Ever wondered why a bad night’s sleep can leave you irritable, anxious or sad? Poor sleep affects our emotions, but its timing also plays a role. Our circadian rhythms are nearly 24-hour cycles that regulate alertness, hormones, body temperature and digestion. Deep inside the brain, a cluster of nerve cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as the body’s master clock. It uses light signals from the eyes to coordinate clocks in other organs, including the brain, liver, heart and gut. When daily routines fall out of sync with this clock, mood can suffer. Research suggests circadian disruption may contribute to mental health challenges. Our internal clock helps regulate hormones, including melatonin and cortisol. Melatonin helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle. Levels stay low during the day, rise in the evening as darkness falls (signalling to the brain that it is time to rest), peak in the middle of the night, and drop off in the morning. Cortisol, which helps us respond to stress, typically rises towards morning. These changes prepare the body for activity and rest, while influencing emotional wellbeing. In a 2024 laboratory study , my colleagues and I investigated whether our internal clocks influence mood independently of everyday activities. We studied 19 healthy adults over 32 hours, measuring mood while minimising changes in their surroundings and behaviour. We found that anxiety-like and depression-like mood were highest at around 8am to 9am, while participants reported greater mental fatigue and lower physical comfort between approximately 6am and 8am. These patterns were linked to their internal biological clocks, suggesting that mood can fluctuate according to biological time, independently of everyday routines. Circadian disruption has also been linked to depression and bipolar disorder, a condition involving episodes of depression and elevated or irritable mood. The relationship also works in both directions. Mental health difficulties can disrupt sleep and circadian rhythms, potentially creating a cycle in which low quality sleep and psychological distress reinforce one another. What happens when our clocks fall out of sync Night shift workers may need to stay awake when their bodies are preparing for sleep and rest when their internal clocks promote alertness. This mismatch is known as circadian misalignment. In a 2020 study , we investigated how this misalignment affected mood in two controlled laboratory experiments involving people with and without shift-work experience. Participants followed schedules designed to simulate day and night shifts while all other behavioural and environmental factors were controlled for, including light exposure, physical activity, food intake and opportunities for sleep. We found that mood and wellbeing reduced when participants’ sleeping and waking schedules were misaligned with their internal body clock. The effects were observed in non-shift workers as well as shift workers. These findings suggest circadian misalignment can influence mood, although larger studies are needed to establish the long-term consequences. Outside the laboratory, many people experience a mismatch known as social jetlag . This occurs when people’s sleep and waking times differ substantially between working days and days off. Artificial light can also affect our internal clocks. Bright light in the evening, including light from electronic screens, can suppress melatonin and delay our sleep time. My research on light sensitivity has highlighted differences between individuals. Some people’s circadian rhythms are much more sensitive to evening light than others, meaning the same exposure may have different effects. Could changing meal times help? Light is the strongest environmental signal for the master clock, but eating also influences the timing of biological processes in other organs. In a 2022 study , my colleagues and I investigated whether changing meal times could reduce the effects of simulated night work on mood. Nineteen healthy volunteers followed carefully controlled schedules designed to mimic night shifts. One group ate during both the day and night, while the other ate only during the daytime. A study of simulated night shifts found that participants who ate during the day and night experienced worsening mood, while those who ate only during the day did not show the same changes. Among participants who ate during both periods, ratings of depression-like mood increased by 26.2% and anxiety-like mood by 16.1% compared with their baseline measurements. We did not observe significant increases in either measure among those who ate only during the daytime. These findings suggest that the timing of meals may influence how circadian disruption affects mood. However, the study involved a small group of healthy volunteers under laboratory conditions. Further research involving shift workers is needed to establish whether eating only during the daytime can help reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression. How to support your body clock Although we may not control our working hours or sleep schedules, some daily habits may help keep our internal clocks aligned. Get morning daylight . Light is the most powerful environmental signal for the master clock. Spending time outdoors after waking can support alertness and help regulate the timing of sleep later. The amount of light needed varies between people. Read more: Tired, irritable and craving carbs? Why darker days affect our bodies and brains Reduce bright light before bed. Dimming household lights and limiting screen use in the evening/night-time may help the body prepare for sleep. The NHS recommends avoiding electronic screens for at least an hour before bedtime. Keep a regular sleep-wake schedule. Going to bed and waking up at reasonably consistent times can help reinforce circadian rhythms. A systematic review associated regular sleep patterns with better health outcomes, including diabetes, heart diseases and depression. Consider food and exercise timing. Consistent and earlier food times may help support the body’s daily rhythms for physical health, although research is needed to establish the best eating schedules for mental health. Regular physical activity can also benefit sleep. A review of studies found that evening exercise generally did not interfere with sleep, although vigorous exercise ending very close to bedtime sometimes did. Protecting sleep and mental health Research suggests that the timing of sleep and daily activities can influence mood, although more evidence is needed to establish whether changing these routines can help prevent or treat mental health conditions. Maintaining consistent routines and getting enough sleep may support emotional wellbeing, but these habits cannot replace appropriate treatment. Anyone experiencing persistent sleep or mood problems should seek medical advice. Understanding how our internal clocks influence mood may eventually offer new ways to support mental health.

articles.title: Could an erectile dysfunction drug offer a new way to treat Alzheimer’s?
articles.summary: A drug developed to treat erectile dysfunction might seem an unlikely treatment for Alzheimer’s disease. But researchers are increasingly interested in whether medicines such as Viagra could also help protect the brain. These drugs affect blood flow and other processes that may play a role in brain health . An experimental drug called AR1001 has produced encouraging results in a large international clinical trial. In one group of people with early Alzheimer’s, the drug was reported to slow the worsening of symptoms by 31% over a year, compared with a placebo. AriBio, a South Korean biotechnology company, announced the results at the 19th Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston, US. A full scientific paper, reviewed by other researchers, has not yet been published. The phase three trial – the final phase of testing in humans – involved 1,535 people with early Alzheimer’s in 13 countries. Participants took either 30mg of AR1001 or a placebo every day for a year. Researchers measured changes in memory, thinking and everyday activities. They looked at two groups: everyone who took part in the trial and a smaller group of 604 people who were not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines to ease their symptoms, such as donepezil or memantine. Only this smaller group saw a 31% reduction in worsening symptoms. Across the whole trial, AR1001 did not produce reliable benefits. How could erectile dysfunction drugs affect the brain? Erectile dysfunction drugs work by blocking an enzyme that normally breaks down a chemical messenger – called cGMP – in the body. This allows cGMP to build up, helping the muscles around blood vessels relax. The vessels widen, allowing more blood to flow through them. This is how the drugs help treat erectile dysfunction. The same chemical messenger also helps brain cells communicate with each other . Researchers think that increasing its levels could help brain cells survive and maintain the connections they need to share information. These connections are essential for learning and memory. Alzheimer’s gradually damages them, making it harder to remember things and think clearly. Researchers hope that AR1001 might help protect some of these connections and slow the damage caused by the disease. However, this is still a theory. The clinical trial does not show that these biological changes explain the reported benefits in people. Some laboratory and animal studies support the idea. In a 2022 study , mice with features of Alzheimer’s disease performed better in memory tests after receiving AR1001. The treatment also reduced levels of amyloid-beta and abnormal tau, two proteins linked to Alzheimer’s. AR1001 belongs to the same family of drugs as Viagra. Other experimental research in mice has found that AR1001 can increase levels of cGMP and a protein that helps brain cells survive. However, results in animals do not always translate into benefits for humans. Interest in this family of drugs has also grown following research in people. A 2024 study followed more than 269,000 men with erectile dysfunction. It found that men prescribed these drugs were 18% less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s than men who were not prescribed them. But this was an observational study, which means it cannot show that the drugs themselves reduced the risk of Alzheimer’s. The two groups may have differed in other ways that influenced the results. A complicated relationship The relationship between erectile dysfunction and Alzheimer’s is complicated. Erectile dysfunction can be associated with conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, which can damage blood vessels. These same conditions are also linked to poorer brain health and a higher risk of dementia . This means that some of the apparent link between erectile dysfunction, its treatments and dementia could be down to shared risk factors affecting blood vessels, rather than a direct effect of the drugs. Erectile dysfunction drugs are not an established treatment for Alzheimer’s, and nothing in these results suggests people should take them to protect their memory. The latest trial does, however, keep alive an interesting possibility: that drugs that improve blood flow and help brain cells communicate might also slow the damage caused by Alzheimer’s. Whether this is the case will depend on the full trial results and further research in people, including studies looking at why the apparent benefit was seen only among those not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines.

articles.summary: New Delhi: Former India off-spinner R Ashwin picked out wicketkeeper-batter Rishabh Pant as the Indian who may have "a chirp or two" behind the stumps about the Sandpaper saga during the home Test series against Australia early next year. The five-match Border-Gavaskar Trophy series between India and Australia will be played at five Indian venues from January 21 to March 3. "Can I be very candid about this? I see just one character in that Indian dressing room who might have a chirp about it, which is Rishabh Pant, standing behind the stumps. He might have a chirp or two," Ashwin said when asked about the possibility of Indian players sledging Australia during the series. "But I'd be very disappointed if I don't see Aussies give it back, if at all, the Indian team resorts to it, because that's what the Aussies are known for," Ashwin said on JioStar. 'Coach can only prepare team but players have to deliver': Gavaskar Ashwin, however, advised the Indian team to be worried about its own dressing room. "And India have their own issues themselves in the Test setup, than be worried about the other dressing room. You take care of your cricket, you're going to end up with good results. It will entirely be dependent on how well India start that series." Australian cricket is in rough waters once again due to the Sandpaper scandal that rocked the game in 2018, following revelations in Usman Khawaja's book and subsequent claims by Cameron Bancroft that the entire team knew about the ball-tampering plot during the infamous third Test in Cape Town. Asked about Cricket Australia banning then captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner for one year in the aftermath of the scandal, Ashwin said, "Culturally, we are very different as a country. As an Indian travelling to Australia, I've often admired their culture and their will to win. Those are things you imbibe from them. "Having said that, I don't think it's the responsibility of the current Australian team to carry the burden of what happened in 2018. Who hasn't made a mistake? Are we all saints sitting here? Hasn't the world made mistakes? "We've had world leaders who have made mistakes, and that's just human nature. To err is human. We need to understand that people will make mistakes. As long as they own up and move on, that's all you can ask for." Ashwin, who retired from international cricket in December 2024 after taking 537 wickets from 106 Tests, lauded Cricket Australia for taking action and sending out a message that leaders must take accountability for their teams. "...when it comes to Cricket Australia, I would give them credit for one thing in this case. They acted upon something like this and got their captain and vice-captain banned, sending out a message that leaders must take accountability for their teams. "In the past, there have been similar instances where the ICC handed a player or a group of players a one-game or a series ban. "But here, Cricket Australia took it to the cleaners. Australian cricketers are held to a certain code of morality and high standards, and Cricket Australia acted upon that." Former Australia opener Matthew Hayden reckoned that with multiple assignments, including the upcoming Border-Gavaskar Trophy, ahead, the conversations will eventually shift to cricket on the field. "Australia will not only be competitive, but will also want to win. Australia has largely been very fair in the way it has gone about its cricketing culture. Very little has disrupted the nature of the Australian winning culture. It's a very in-your-face culture. R Ashwin for playing four frontline seamers in New Zealand Tests "It will confront issues inside the change room collectively. That's why I'm really disappointed in this 2018 mob that couldn't do it. Largely, the game has already moved on... and will move on very quickly. The cricket will speak for itself, and it will speak volumes." Former India pacer Irfan Pathan felt the best way for the Australian team to handle the Sandpaper saga was to not talk about it. "If the players keep answering questions and going into a detailed analysis of what happened eight years ago, they will be in trouble. The best thing for them to do is leave it at that and move on. "As far as integrity is concerned, people will always question them, no matter what they do. Even if Cricket Australia decides to conduct an investigation now for the sake of the people and media back home, this will continue to be discussed for even 10, 20 or 30 years from now."
