articles.title: Kerala HC quashes suspension of 16 Kalady Sanskrit varsity students, orders special exams
articles.summary: The Kerala High Court, on Monday, November 23, quashed the suspension of 16 students of Sree Sankaracharya University of Sanskrit (SSUS), Kalady, and set aside the disciplinary inquiry report against them, ruling that the University had violated the principles of natural justice while initiating action over a campus protest. Justice PV Kunhikrishnan directed the University to allow the students to return to the campus and attend regular classes immediately. The court also ordered the University to conduct separate examinations within six weeks for students who missed their examinations due to the suspension. The court passed the order while allowing a writ petition filed by Archana PS and 15 other students. The judge found serious procedural lapses in the University's inquiry, including failure to communicate specific charges to the students, recording witness statements in their absence, and denying them access to complaints and an opportunity to cross-examine witnesses. The court also observed that the inquiry committee had exceeded its mandate by relying on unrelated complaints and the students' antecedents. The inquiry report was not a "speaking order", as it reached conclusions without adequately discussing the evidence, the court noted. The University had argued that the students could approach the Students’ Grievance Redressal Committee or the Ombudsperson. However, the court rejected the contention, observing that such a remedy would amount to an appeal from "Caesar to Caesar's wife", given that the bodies were appointed by the University and Vice-Chancellor Ciza Thomas herself was an aggrieved party. The 16 students, all members of the Students Federation of India (SFI), were suspended on September 1, following a protest held on August 13. The University had alleged that the protesters staged a mock funeral of the Vice-Chancellor, manhandled her, and attempted to damage her vehicle as she left the office following a Syndicate meeting. The students, however, maintained that they had staged a mock funeral for non-functioning stage lights. The protest was part of a series of demonstrations that began on July 22 over various grievances. The students had raised issues including 27 vacant lecturer posts, non-issuance of printed certificates, inadequate infrastructure, and delays in fellowship payments. Protest, suspension, legal battle: What is happening at Kerala’s Sankaracharya University The suspension had prevented some students from appearing for examinations that began on November 4. The students initially approached the High Court seeking permission to write the examinations. Although a single bench granted interim relief on October 30, a division bench subsequently set aside the order, citing the absence of pleadings concerning their eligibility under the University's minimum attendance and internal assessment requirements. The students then approached the Supreme Court challenging the division bench's decision. While declining to interfere, the apex court urged the High Court to expedite the hearing of their challenge to the suspension. The University had given an undertaking before the Supreme Court that it would conduct special examinations if the suspension orders were revoked. The High Court directed the University to honour that undertaking and conduct the examinations within six weeks. It also clarified that any fresh disciplinary inquiry should not be used as a reason to delay the special examinations. The court granted the University liberty to initiate a fresh inquiry in accordance with the law but made it clear that the students should not be suspended during the proceedings. Further, the court said that if the students were found guilty in a fresh inquiry, the 84 days they had already spent under suspension must be taken into account while deciding the punishment. During an earlier hearing on November 11, Justice Kunhikrishnan had questioned the University's decision to keep the students suspended for nearly 60 days and demand an apology from them. "I am not accepting what they have done, but they have suffered. They have been out for 60 days. Assume for argument that there is misconduct. Isn't this 60 days enough?" the court had orally observed. Justice Kunhikrishnan cited instances of political leaders showing leniency towards student protesters, including former prime minister Manmohan Singh, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and former Kerala chief minister EMS Namboodiripad. The judge urged the authorities to consider forgiveness rather than allowing disciplinary action to destroy students' academic careers. "Forgiveness is not a sin; it is an affirmation of human dignity," the court concluded.

The female falcon, Alang, first reached Somalia in 101 hours, that is four days and five hours. She was followed by Apapang. Amur falcons are the small pigeon-sized birds which migrate in a large numbers every year. The male is blackish grey in colour and the female bird is brighter in colour, both having whitish underwing lining. The female is larger in size than the male. How did the COP31 climate agreement fall apart – and what happens now?
articles.summary: Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, have come to an end – but not as we might have hoped. Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt , shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners. In a year of unprecedented climate disasters , a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming , the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment . Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right. These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement. Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process – or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards. Chris Bowen, the COP31 president of negotiations and Australia’s Minister for Climate Change, speaks to the media after the final session during the second overtime day of the climate talks. No mention of the ‘F’ word For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable. Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “ transition away from fossil fuels ”, marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations. The Dubai text was hailed as “ the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era ”. But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Turkey. In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text. Australia and Turkey proposed a compromise – no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy”. This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text. Brazil took a different approach to the same problem last year. In a bid to break the deadlock, Brazil committed to develop a global strategy to phase out fossil fuels outside the formal negotiating agenda. The roadmap was launched at this year’s summit in Turkey and managed to attract support from big fossil fuel producers such as India, Germany and Nigeria. Countries across the European Union are launching similar roadmaps . Frustration over fossil fuels at COP31 is likely to lead more nations to go outside official talks to progress phase-out efforts. Earlier this year, 57 nations attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland . Neither the Turkish hosts nor their Australian partners seemed keen to mention fossil fuels. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was untroubled by the optics of announcing two huge new oilfields in Turkey in his speech at the summit opening. While Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the existential risks to Pacific countries from climate change, he made no commitment to stop approving new Australian coal and gas projects. Both leaders much preferred to talk about electrification, namely the flagship “ 35 by 35” electrification pledge . The goal here is to boost electricity’s share of final energy use globally from around 23% at present to 35% by 2035. Efforts to embed this goal in the cover text failed. But the electrification pledge drew strong support outside official negotiations. More than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on , including the European Union and China . Activist Greta Thunberg attends a protest at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. The “COP of action” fails to deliver This year’s climate summit was billed as an “ implementation COP” , focused on delivering the pledges countries had already made to address climate change. Overseen by Australia in its role as “ president of negotiations ”, the formal talks largely focused on the actions countries are taking to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, whether their response is sufficiently urgent and whether funds aimed at supporting the most vulnerable countries are adequate. It was abundantly obvious that longstanding divisions had not been overcome. Developed countries called for emissions to be cut faster, while developing countries responded by pointing to a lack of financial support to do so. African countries, in particular, stressed that an “implementation COP” was meaningless if rich nations failed to provide the actual resources needed to act. Participants sit around awaiting news of negotiations on the final day of the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey. Despite the general gloom, these talks did achieve progress in a few areas. Nations moved forwards on supporting a just transition (shifting to clean energy fairly) via a “ phased approach ”, as well as improving alignment in climate adaptation , which will help the poorest nations to implement their adaptation plans. But broader efforts to find a way forward on the Paris Agreement’s Global Goal on Adaptation were left unresolved. Decisions stalled in many negotiating rooms in the face of hard “red lines” declared by different blocs of countries. Countries failed to reach any agreement on the vital question of cutting emissions, after Saudia Arabia and Russia blocked a proposed decision. Both are among the world’s top fossil fuel exporting nations. This failure has left the world without any dedicated negotiating process on cutting emissions under the Paris Agreement. It’s possible nations could agree to renew a work program on climate mitigation at next year’s COP32 talks in Ethiopia. What about money for adaptation? Who pays for the costs of climate change has long been a contentious point. Developing countries face the brunt of damage from climate change, but have emitted far less – and have much less money to spend on adaptation. Ahead of COP31, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said talks on new climate finance commitments were “dead in the water” . He urged delegates to focus on implementing existing pledges rather than try for fresh funding. The summit failed to meet even these low expectations. No concrete progress was achieved on the goal of tripling funds for climate adaptation pledged last year at COP30 in Brazil. Ahead of the summit, the Australian government flagged the need to boost global contributions to the official Pacific climate fund . This, too, didn’t eventuate. Rich nations – including Australia – merely re-announced their existing pledges, leaving the Pacific fund A$450 million short of its 2026 target of $749 million. Ironically, the most notable pledge came from the Solomon Islands, a small Pacific nation. Prime Minister Matthew Wale pledged $600,000 to the global Green Climate Fund. “The Pacific did not create this crisis,” he declared. “But we will not stand by and wait for others to act”. A few new commitments arrived by the end of the two week summit from nations such as Canada and Norway . Press and participants watch as a man dressed as a dinosaur performs as part of the Fossil Of The Day award at the COP31 UN climate summit. Defending the science Unusually, climate science was front and centre at COP31. This year, a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries has been obstructing the publication of key scientific reports from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. This year marks the first UN summit since it was officially confirmed the world will overshoot the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal by 2030. With the collapse of support for the cover text, statements supporting release of the latest climate science didn’t get approval. All that remained were technical conclusions which “expressed utmost concern” that climate impacts will continue to increase with every increment of global warming. IPCC chair Jim Skea at the opening ceremony of COP31. Previously, he described the stymied outcome of the meeting in Ethiopia as frustrating and disappointing. Australia on the global stage COP31 gave Australia a unique global role. After being outmanoeuvred in their bid to host the summit, Australia secured a role in overseeing negotiations . Australian Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and his team had the unenviable task of seeking consensus between 195 countries and the European Union. After the cover text was rejected, Bowen declared Australia had left “ nothing on the field ” but had faced “unbridgeable red lines.” Hours beforehand, Fijian Climate Minister Lynda Tabuya acknowledged Bowen’s efforts , noting the failure was “not yours to carry […] it is the responsibility of all parties.” Are COP summits still worthwhile? This year’s climate summit took the unenviable record of the longest ever . With consensus seemingly impossible, some civil society representatives dubbed it “ the worst COP ever .” Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blamed “powerful fossil fuel interests”, including fossil fuel exporters and corporate lobbyists . Some nations are now calling for urgent reform to negotiations long paralysed by vetoes and disconnected from science. Unfortunately, any change to official voting processes would itself require a consensus decision. Consensus is hard to achieve, but powerful. The power of the Paris Agreement draws on the fact it represents the view of nearly every country – big or small, rich or poor. COP31 President Murat Kurum began the summit expressing hopes this year’s talks would leave a legacy of “ working together .” That was a false hope. A more realistic hope is that the collapse of consensus may be the shock the world needs to change course. As former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has said, we should not see the refusal of more than 130 countries to sign an inadequate deal as a failure. Rather, it might be “ a sign of courage ”.

Students commonly make foreign-currency payments for: ● Accommodation deposits and rent ● Groceries and local transport ● Books and study materials ● Online subscriptions ● Restaurants and everyday purchases ● Emergency expenses Not every provider accepts cards, so students should check payment methods before relying on a card for recurring expenses. How does forex markup affect student spending? Many cards add a foreign exchange markup of up to 3.5% when a transaction is processed in another currency and additional GST of 18% on the markup fee on eligible spends . A purchase in dollars, euros or pounds is converted into INR using the applicable exchange rate, after which the issuer may add its markup. Regular payments can make even a small markup noticeable. How can a zero-forex card reduce costs? A 0 forex markup credit card does not charge the issuer's forex markup on eligible foreign-currency transactions, subject to applicable terms. Potential savings may arise from: ● Shopping and groceries ● Restaurants and transport ● Educational purchases ● International online subscriptions However, zero forex does not fix the exchange rate. Currency movements can still affect the final INR amount. What should students compare before choosing a card? Forex savings should be considered alongside the card's other costs and benefits. Students should also check spending conditions, exclusions and limits attached to specific benefits. What other costs should students watch? Even with a 0 forex markup credit card , other charges may apply. These include: ● ATM withdrawal charges ● Dynamic currency conversion (DCC) ● Interest on unpaid balances ● Applicable service charges When paying abroad, you may sometimes be given the option to pay in INR instead of the local currency. This is called Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC). If you choose INR, the merchant or ATM converts the amount using its applicable exchange rate and charges, which may differ from paying in the local currency. articles.title: Bangladesh court orders interim curbs on social media for children under 16
articles.summary: Dhaka: A Bangladeshi court has directed the authorities to frame mandatory interim guidelines to prevent children below 16 years of age from accessing social media platforms and ordered the formation of an independent expert committee to examine the impact of algorithm-driven content feeds on minors. The High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh issued the directives on Sunday while passing an order on a writ petition that questioned the government's failure to formulate a national policy regulating social media access for children under 16 , the Prothom Alo newspaper reported. The bench comprising Justices Sikder Mahmudur Razi and Fatema Anwar directed the Secretary of the Posts and Telecommunications Division and the Chairman of the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission, among other respondents, to take necessary steps. Bangladesh violence: 30 houses torched amid attacks on Awami League leaders, activists It also ordered the immediate formation of a committee comprising cybersecurity specialists, child psychologists, paediatricians and legal experts to assess the structural impact of algorithm-controlled feeds on children. The move comes amid growing international concerns over the impact of social media on children's mental health, physical well-being and development, with governments across the globe increasingly considering age-based restrictions and stricter safeguards against potentially harmful online content. The committee will examine how algorithm-based recommendation systems influence children's behaviour, exposure to online content and overall development, and submit its assessment to help shape regulatory measures. The writ petition was filed earlier this month by Supreme Court lawyer Mohammad Faisal Dastagir, who appeared before the court in person. The absence of a regulatory framework had left children below 16 exposed to unrestricted social media use, potentially affecting their mental and physical development, Dastagir was quoted as saying by Prothom Alo. Citing research highlighting health concerns, including impaired eyesight, among children exposed to excessive screen time, he argued that a national policy was necessary to regulate their access to social media. BNP, Awami League supporters clash in Bangladesh amid political unrest The court also directed the authorities to explain why their failure to establish an independent committee to assess the structural impact of algorithm-controlled feeds on minors and formulate a national policy restricting social media access for children under 16 should not be declared illegal and beyond their lawful authority, the report said. Several countries across the world are tightening regulations governing children's access to social media. Australia became the first country to enforce a minimum age of 16 for accounts on major social media platforms in December 2025, requiring platforms to take reasonable steps to prevent under-16s from creating or retaining accounts. Indonesia banned children under 16 from having accounts on "high-risk" social media and online platforms starting on March 28, 2026, making it the first country in Southeast Asia to introduce such restrictions. Malaysia, too, began enforcing age-verification requirements in June 2026, barring children below 16 from opening social media accounts and requiring existing users to verify their age. The UK plans to ban children under 16 from major social media platforms starting in spring 2027, with initial regulations expected to be laid before Parliament by December 2026. It is also considering overnight curfews for teens aged 16 and 17 and blocking infinite-scroll mechanisms for kids. Canada introduced a bill in parliament in June, proposing a minimum age of 16 for holding social media accounts. The proposed legislation is yet to become law. Bangladesh issues nationwide alert against possible attacks on police vehicles Brazil enacted rules in 2026 requiring age verification and parental account linking for users under 16. The European Commission has proposed the EU KIDS Act in September to ban children under 13 from social media and set 15 as the minimum age for independent accounts. Countries such as France, Greece, Turkey, Spain, Poland, New Zealand, Denmark, and Slovenia have drafted restrictions aimed primarily at under-15s, while Austria has proposed an under-14 ban.

Rasa Theatre’s Many A Thousand Years ponders on existential dread and the ache of waiting
articles.summary: Many A Thousand Years (English) Night after night, when the curtains fall on their performances, two actors meet near a rock and wait. Nothing happens, nobody comes, nobody goes; it's awful. As it was for Vladimir and Estragon in Waiting for Godot , so it is for Mano and Gomi in Many A Thousand Years . Except, there is no Godot to look forward to, even if in vain. The fourth major production by Kochi-based Rasa Theatre Collective, Many A Thousand Years attempts to explore the ‘waiting’ that is central to human existence, inspired by Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot. It is written by Aparna Ashok and directed by Rahul Thomas. Rahul plays Mano, a theatre actor who transforms into Hamlet on stage, seeking an answer to the centuries-old question: to be or not to be? Each night, as Mano washes off his makeup and removes his costumes, he is joined by another actor, Gomi, played by Abraham Vadakkan. Day in and day out, Gomi plays Bhima, who, with a swing of his mace, breaks Duryodhana’s thigh in the Mahabharata . The audience erupts in applause, the curtains fall, and Gomi resumes the wait for the next day. Monotony is the norm of their lives. The play progresses through several nights during which the same two actors wait at the same spot and discuss the same things. One night becomes indistinguishable from the next, and neither of them seem to know what they are waiting for. It is absurd theatre, and so the dialogues and gestures are bound to be repetitive and illogical. The play makes an attempt to lay bare the psyche of the artist who craves both adulation and meaning. Gomi revels in the appreciation his craft receives, hungers for more, and seems aware that he is larger than himself when playing Bhima on stage. Even when off stage, he refuses to take off a bangle that is part of his Bhima costume. Mano seems to be chasing a perfection that is just beyond reach when he is shown trying different modulations for the same line or looking for a lost hat that was perfect for him. The metatheatrical elements are not limited to the existential questions raised by the actors played by actors. The ‘stage’ leaves them notes, asking them to ‘Try again' or ‘Prepare’. The fourth wall is broken on more than one instance to invite the audience to ponder on the endless waiting that is life. The invitations to join the existential reflections were rather in your face throughout the play, not just when the fourth wall was broken. There were one too many literary references, letting us know that the play intends to evoke existential dread in the audience. It seemed weighed down by the gravity of its philosophical questions, which were almost spelt out for the audience through the dialogue on many instances. Unfortunately, the forced efforts only seemed to have the opposite effect on the viewer. One wishes the play wasn’t so conscious of its absurdist nature; that it would leave room for the audience to think and ask their own questions. The attempts at humour too fell flat on more than one occasion. But that is not to say the play is without merits. There were several clever elements, like the arch drawn on the floor with white pebbles within which the performance unfolds, serving as a figurative salt circle marking the boundary between the artist and the world. Mano grabs a handful of pebbles on a few occasions and spreads them over the arch, as though reinforcing the boundary. At one point, Gomi tries to push past the limit, the arch of pebbles expanding to outline his straying feet. But such details may have escaped the notice of viewers beyond the first row, given that the stage and the audience were all seated at the same level. Towards the end, Gomi discovers that the rock they sat near was scribbled with the names of others who had waited there before them. The actors read out the scribbled names, which include Albert Camus, Beckett, Vaikom Muhammad Basheer, and several others, as well as the names of audience members. ‘You are also waiting,’ the play tells the audience, again. But despite the bluntness of the message, it was a smart use of a stage property. Both Rahul and Abraham bested each other in acting. Sujith V and Aravind, who handled the music and lights, respectively, made sure that the play was brought together well. The costumes by Merianna Kurian also deserve special mention. Many A Thousand Nights premiered at the Ala Centre for Culture in Ernakulam’s Mulamthuruthy on November 22. Rasa Theatre Collective’s previous productions include Niyamavarthanam and Guards at the Taj . Disclaimer: This review was not paid for or commissioned by anyone associated with the play. Neither TNM nor any of its reviewers have any sort of business relationship with the producers or any other members of its cast and crew.

articles.summary: Wellington: India skipper Shubman Gill expressed his frustration over the flat deck doled out for the opening Test while his New Zealand counterpart Tom Latham too felt it was not a typical Basin Reserve pitch after the opening game saw 1327 runs being scored with literally bowler after bowler made to toil. “Yes, there is a little frustration that the match did not get the desired result. But this is also part of the game. For the past 6-7 years, there haven’t been many draws in Tests. Earlier, if a team went to play 5-match series matches, they used to draw about 2 matches. It was a little common then, but now it is not that common. That’s why we are not used to draws. You do feel frustrated about the pitch,” said Gill at the post match press conference. Ind vs NZ Test series | Fifteen overs to go, five wickets to take. Why did India give up? “When we started playing the Test match, we thought there will be a lot more in the wicket. I think on Day 3, 4 and 5 it just went flatter and flatter. There were no scallops in the wicket. Or there was no impact of overs being bowled on the wicket. Or even the days being played. The wicket just got slower and slower. So, having seen that, I think it was not a great Test wicket, especially if you want results. But having said that, now we talk about results a lot more because of the WTC.” 'Ball plays a big role': Indian captain Shubham Gill questions continued saliva ban in cricket Despite the draw, Gill felt fourth-placed India can still make it to the top two and earn a place in the WTC final next year. “I think in this cycle, I don't know exactly how many, but I think we were playing around 18-20 matches. So, I think that's a lot of matches If you play well, and even from now on, if we play well, and if we win 5 out of the next 6, I think we should be in a good position to qualify for the WTC.” Latham too felt surprised by the flatness of the pitch. “It's probably not the traditional base and surface that we've been presented with over the last few years. I guess a traditional Basin wicket is where it keeps its pace and bounce and we probably didn't necessarily see that from day two onwards, but again I've spoken about it before, it's a little bit cliche, but it's about trying to adapt to conditions as best we can.”

articles.summary: The Bengaluru police on Sunday, November 22 stopped Andhra Pradesh Congress chief YS Sharmila from proceeding to a disputed family property in Yelahanka. Her brother, former Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister YS Jagan Mohan Reddy, currently resides at the property. Sharmila was travelling from Kempegowda International Airport towards the bungalow with her mother, YS Vijayamma, and other family members when police intercepted her near Air Force Cross around 6 pm. Officials showed her a court order restraining her from interfering with possession of the property. “There is a court order, a permanent injunction, stating that she should not go there. As soon as the order was shown, she left the place,” Deputy Commissioner of Police G K Mithun Kumar told PTI. According to media reports, the police had received information about Sharmila‘s movement towards the property and intervened to prevent a law and order situation. Sharmila reportedly told the police that she did not intend to enter the bungalow but only wanted to pass by it on her way to a restaurant on Thanisandra Main Road. The Andhra Pradesh Congress said Sharmila questioned the police for stopping her from visiting what she considers her residence. “Police blocked APCC chief YS Sharmila Reddy at Air Force Cross in Bengaluru. Police blocked her from going to the Yelahanka residence. The PCC chief asked police what was wrong in going to her residence,” the party said in a statement issued in Amaravati. The intervention followed an interim injunction issued by the Senior Civil Judge‘s court in Devanahalli on November 21. The order restrains Sharmila, her family members and people acting on her behalf from interfering with Silicon Builders Private Limited‘s possession of the property. The injunction was issued in a suit filed by Silicon Builders, which claims to be in lawful possession of the premises under a lease agreement. The company alleged that Sharmila and people acting on her behalf had attempted to interfere with its possession. The dispute is part of a long-running disagreement between Sharmila and Jagan over family assets. In 2024, Jagan approached the National Company Law Tribunal seeking to nullify the transfer of shares in Saraswati Power and Industries Private Limited to Sharmila and their mother, YS Vijayamma. He also wrote to Sharmila stating that he would not honour a memorandum of understanding between them. The latest dispute over the Yelahanka property intensified after Jagan declined to allow Sharmila to host her daughter‘s wedding at the bungalow. In an October 9 letter, he cited security concerns over the number of guests and service providers who would enter the premises, as well as the circulation of photographs and videos of the property. Sharmila subsequently shifted the wedding, scheduled for November 25, to Hyderabad. She has maintained that the Yelahanka property belongs entirely to her under the family‘s division of assets.

articles.title: UoH students launch protest seeking professor’s termination over casteist remarks
articles.summary: University of Hyderabad students have launched an indefinite protest demanding the termination of Dr Vijaya Ramdas Mandala, a faculty member in the History Department, over his alleged derogatory remarks about Dalit students in an email exchange. The remarks were allegedly made after a former student expressed hesitation regarding incorporating certain suggestions made by Vijaya Ramdas into his research because of ethical concerns. The incident took place in April but came to light only recently. The protest has been called by the Students’ Union, which comprises various student groups, including the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), the Ambedkar Students’ Association, the Dalit Students’ Union,and the Tribal Students’ Forum. Students have been staging a sit-in outside the Social Sciences building, demanding Vijaya Ramdas’s termination. “We will not call off the protest until Vijaya Ramdas is terminated,” PhD student Aditya Rao told TNM. “We had protested earlier too, but no concrete action was taken against him,” he added. The screenshots of an email exchange were shown to TNM by student activists. Through the emails, Vijaya Ramdas contacted Sandeep (name changed), who is a PhD student at Manchester Business School, about corrections to his chapter for a forthcoming book by Bloomsbury India. In the email thread, the History professor refers to former students from the Dalit community as “untouchables” more than once. He also refers to another student studying at Nottingham as “Dalit untouchable idiot”. The email exchange, which took place between April 14 and 16, grew increasingly tense after Sandeep said he would need the permission of his current university to anonymise the people he was being asked to name in the research, to avoid being flagged for ethical violations. “It will take months to get an ethical review committee's decision from the University of Manchester to write the names asked for in my chapter and publish it as a PhD student of the University,” Sandeep said. Vijaya Ramdas responded: “At Indian business schools, or even at Harvard Business School or Rotman Business School, your chapter discussing managerial and business people would not have been a problem. It's not a History Department perspective, as 99.5% of History departments worldwide do not deal with business history.” Sandeep then pointed to another obstacle in the research, saying that one of the students who is part of his research would need approval to conduct research in India. He also said the researcher was unclear about the archival sources. Vijaya Ramdas responded: “The recent German PhD who comes from an untouchable Dalit background also said to me the same thing about his collection of archives in India.” He further wrote: “A large chunk of the Indian population is from non-Aryan and non-wealthy backgrounds, including backward states like Bihar and Jharkhand, which resemble some countries in Africa on the political map of India and across the globe. This also happened to another Dalit untouchable idiot at Nottingham, who is working part-time in a hotel in England after his post-UK PhD (sic).” Vijaya Ramdas also called Sandeep “anti-Indian”, threatened to withhold academic support, and said his chapter would not be included in the book. He said people from poverty-ridden backgrounds developed “Pakistani-centric thinking (not knowing that one cannot emulate class, one should be born in a high class and culture) in a country known as Mini-Pakistan.” “I am terminating further communication with you, but also will not provide academic support from third-rate, poverty-ridden idiots from Bihar and Jharkhand henceforth,” he concluded. In addition to seeking Vijaya Ramdas’s termination, the students have called for his arrest under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. They have also demanded that Bloomsbury India suspend its ongoing project with him and that caste sensitisation workshops be held across the University. In a statement issued to the media on November 23, Dr Vijaya Ramadas M stated that the communication in question was 'unauthorised, without his knowledge and awareness.' "It is categorically stated that the email dated 16 April 2026, which allegedly passed through my personal Gmail account, was neither authored nor transmitted with my knowledge or consent," he added. (An earlier version of this article did not carry Vijaya Ramdas' response as he hadn't responded at the time of publishing this article.)
